summary: Daniel 12 closes the visions with promised deliverance during an unmatched time of trouble. It speaks of awakening from the dust, the shining of the wise, sealed words, limited suffering, unexplained day counts, and Daniel's own rest and future inheritance. The chapter ends with Daniel told to go his way rather than master every detail.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the book's final movement from persecution to deliverance, resurrection, and waiting. It also shows Daniel himself still limited in understanding, which matters for reading the visions with restraint.

context.author: The visions speak in Daniel's first-person voice, while the book does not name a final editor; traditional and critical readers differ on authorship and date.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: Narratively set from the sixth-century BC exile into Persian rule; most critical scholarship dates the final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167-164 BC, while traditional readings place Daniel's authorship earlier.
context.setting: The book's stories are set in Babylonian and Persian courts; the visions reach toward the persecution associated with Antiochus IV Epiphanes.
context.literaryForm: Apocalyptic vision with heavenly disclosure, symbolic time periods, and unresolved mystery.

outline.heading: Deliverance and awakening
outline.note: Michael stands for Daniel's people; trouble is followed by deliverance, awakening, shining wisdom, and a command to seal the book until the time of the end.

outline.heading: The question of duration
outline.note: Daniel sees two others by the river, and one asks how long the wonders will last; the man clothed in linen gives a solemn timed answer.

outline.heading: Daniel still does not understand
outline.note: Daniel asks about the outcome, but he is told to go his way because the words remain sealed; the chapter contrasts the wicked with those who are wise.

outline.heading: Numbered days and waiting
outline.note: Two day counts are given after the removal of the continual burnt offering and the setting up of the abomination that makes desolate.

outline.heading: Daniel's own end
outline.note: The final word sends Daniel on his way, promising rest and a future standing in his inheritance.

keyVerses.text: “At that time Michael will stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there will be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time. At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.
keyVerses.why: This opens the chapter's final crisis with both severe trouble and promised deliverance.

keyVerses.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's clearest statement of awakening beyond death and divided outcomes.

keyVerses.text: I heard, but I didn’t understand. Then I said, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?”
keyVerses.why: Daniel's lack of understanding sets a limit on how confidently later readers should claim to solve every detail.

keyVerses.text: “But go your way until the end; for you will rest, and will stand in your inheritance at the end of the days.”
keyVerses.why: The book ends by directing Daniel toward rest, endurance, and future inheritance rather than complete explanation.

questions.question: Who is Michael in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter calls Michael “the great prince who stands for the children of your people.” It does not stop to explain his full identity or rank here. The point within the chapter is that Daniel's people are not pictured as abandoned during the time of trouble.

questions.question: What is “the book” in verse 1?
questions.answer: Verse 1 says deliverance belongs to “everyone who is found written in the book.” The chapter does not define the book further, so it is best to say only that it represents those counted among the delivered. Later traditions connect this language with divine records, but that is reception beyond the chapter's own explanation.

questions.question: Is verse 2 talking about resurrection?
questions.answer: The verse says that many who “sleep in the dust of the earth will awake.” It then names different outcomes: “everlasting life” and “shame and everlasting contempt.” Readers commonly understand this as resurrection language, though interpreters debate how it relates to other biblical images of national restoration and final judgment.

questions.question: Who are “those who are wise”?
questions.answer: The chapter says they will understand and will shine, and it links them with turning many to righteousness. It does not describe them as military victors or political rulers. In Daniel's wider final visions, wisdom is associated with endurance and insight under pressure, but this chapter keeps the description brief.

questions.question: Why is Daniel told to shut up and seal the book?
questions.answer: Verse 4 tells Daniel to “shut up the words and seal the book” until “the time of the end,” and verse 9 repeats that the words are “shut up and sealed.” The command presents the revelation as preserved but not fully open for immediate mastery. It fits the chapter's pattern: Daniel receives real words, yet he does not understand everything.

questions.question: What does “a time, times, and a half” mean?
questions.answer: Verse 7 gives this phrase as an answer to “How long will it be to the end of these wonders?” The chapter itself does not convert the phrase into a modern calendar unit. Readers differ over the exact calculation, but the phrase clearly presents the suffering as measured and limited rather than endless.

questions.question: Why does Daniel ask again if an answer has already been given?
questions.answer: Daniel says, “I heard, but I didn’t understand.” His question is not treated as rebellion; it shows the gap between hearing a revelation and grasping its outcome. The answer he receives sends him forward without satisfying every question.

questions.question: What are the 1,290 and 1,335 days?
questions.answer: Verses 11-12 connect the numbers with the time when the continual burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up. The chapter gives the numbers but does not explain the difference between them. Interpreters debate the exact historical or symbolic calculation; the chapter's plain emphasis is on waiting through a bounded period.

questions.question: What happens to Daniel at the end?
questions.answer: Daniel is told, “go your way until the end.” The final sentence says he will rest and will stand in his inheritance at the end of the days. The chapter does not describe the mechanics of that promise, but it places Daniel himself within the hope he has been shown.

glossary.def: The great prince who stands for Daniel's people in the time of trouble.
The severe crisis named in verse 1, described as unlike any since there was a nation.
One outcome for some who awake from the dust of the earth in verse 2.
The horizon until which the words are shut up and sealed in verses 4 and 9.
The regular offering whose removal is tied to the day count in verse 11.
The desecrating thing set up in verse 11; the chapter names it but does not explain all details.
